section-73: The idea of 'Weltliteratur' (world literature) was popularised by the German writer Johann Wolfgang von Goethe in 1827, who believed that national literature was becoming less important and that the age of world literature was beginning. Today the field includes works in translation from Africa, Asia, Latin America, Europe, Australia and the Americas.

World literature helps readers understand different cultures, compare themes such as identity, colonialism, migration, gender and faith across traditions, and see how texts change meaning when translated and read in new contexts.
section-74: David Damrosch, an American scholar, wrote 'What Is World Literature?' (2003) and 'How to Read World Literature' (2009). He defines world literature as 'all literary works that circulate beyond their culture of origin, either in translation or in their original language'. A work becomes world literature when it is actively read in a different literary system.

He argues that world literature is 'writing that gains in translation', and that it is not a fixed canon but a mode of reading. Readers should consider the original cultural context, the role of translation, and how the work speaks to their own time and place. His chapters discuss reading across time, across cultures, in translation, and in a postcolonial and global context.
section-75: Judith Wright (1915-2000) was an Australian poet and activist for Aboriginal rights and the environment. A bora ring is a circular ceremonial ground where Aboriginal people performed initiation rites. In the poem, the songs, dances and stories ('the song is gone; the dance is secret with the dancers in the earth') have vanished.

Only the grass, the trees and the 'grass-overgrown' ring remain; the 'hunter is gone' and the 'spear is broken'. The final stanza alludes to the guilt of the white settlers, comparing it to the 'first blood' of Cain. Themes: loss of Aboriginal culture due to colonisation, memory, guilt and the relationship between land and people.
section-76: Margaret Atwood (born 1939) is a Canadian poet and novelist ('The Handmaid's Tale'). 'A Sad Child' (1995) is addressed to 'you' - a sad child or young person. The speaker says 'You're sad because you're sad. It's psychic. It's the age. It's chemical', mocking the common explanations and remedies (seeing a shrink, taking a pill, hugging your sadness).

The speaker admits that everyone feels unloved at times and that one will never be the 'favourite child'. The ending suggests that in moments of crisis, such as an accident, we all become the same and lose the separate self ('the light that never flickers'). Themes: depression, loneliness, the search for love and the shared condition of human suffering. The tone is frank, ironic and compassionate.
section-77: Syed Amanuddin (1934-2013) was an Indian poet writing in English who lived in the United States. The term 'Indo-Anglian' was used for Indian writing in English, and some critics considered it imitative or inferior.

In the poem the speaker rejects the label because it suggests he is neither fully Indian nor fully English. He asserts that his poetry expresses his own identity and that English, though a foreign language, has become his own medium. Themes: identity, language, postcolonial self-assertion, and the freedom of the poet from labels imposed by critics.
section-78: Fyodor Dostoevsky (1821-1881) was a great Russian novelist ('Crime and Punishment', 'The Brothers Karamazov'). In this short story (1848), the narrator attends a children's Christmas party. He observes Julian Mastakovich, a wealthy, important man, who learns that an eleven-year-old girl will receive a dowry of three hundred thousand roubles. He begins to calculate and flirts with the child in a disturbing way, and harshly treats a poor boy who plays with her.

Five years later, the narrator sees Julian Mastakovich marrying the girl, now sixteen, in a church; she looks sad and pale. The narrator remarks that he had calculated well. Themes: greed, exploitation of children, social hypocrisy and the power of money. The narrator's ironic tone exposes the corruption of upper-class society.
section-79: Katherine Mansfield (1888-1923), a New Zealand-born modernist writer, published 'A Cup of Tea' in 1922. Rosemary Fell is rich, modern and fashionable. After visiting an antique shop and wishing to buy an expensive box, she meets a poor young girl, Miss Smith, who asks for the price of a cup of tea. Excited by the idea of being like a heroine in a novel, Rosemary takes her home.

She feeds the girl and plans to help her, but when her husband Philip says the girl is 'astonishingly pretty', Rosemary becomes jealous, gives the girl three pounds and sends her away. Later she asks Philip, 'Am I pretty?'. Themes: class difference, superficial charity, jealousy, insecurity and the position of women. Mansfield uses free indirect discourse, irony and an open ending.
section-80: Khaled Hosseini's novel (2003) is narrated by Amir, a wealthy Pashtun boy in Kabul. His loyal friend Hassan is a Hazara servant boy. After Amir wins a kite-flying tournament, Hassan runs the last cut kite for him ('For you, a thousand times over') but is assaulted by the bully Assef. Amir witnesses it but does nothing, and out of guilt he frames Hassan for theft, forcing Hassan and his father Ali to leave.

After the Soviet invasion, Amir and his father Baba flee to America. Years later, Rahim Khan calls Amir to Pakistan, saying 'There is a way to be good again', and reveals that Hassan was Amir's half-brother and has been killed by the Taliban. Amir rescues Hassan's son Sohrab from Assef and brings him to America. Themes: guilt and redemption, friendship and betrayal, father-son relationships, ethnic discrimination and the history of Afghanistan.
section-82: Origin of the idea: Goethe's concept of 'Weltliteratur' (1827) imagined literature as a global exchange among nations. Marx and Engels also noted that national one-sidedness was becoming impossible and a world literature was arising.

Damrosch's approach: David Damrosch defines world literature as works that circulate beyond their culture of origin, in translation or in the original. For him it is a mode of circulation and reading rather than a fixed set of masterpieces; works 'gain in translation' by entering new contexts. He emphasises reading across time and cultures, the role of translation, and awareness of both the source culture and the reader's own culture.

Importance: World literature broadens our understanding of humanity, encourages comparison of themes like colonialism, identity, migration, gender and faith, and helps break the dominance of Western or national canons. It also highlights postcolonial voices.

Challenges: Translation may lose cultural nuances; readers may misunderstand texts outside their context; and market forces may decide which texts circulate. Careful, informed reading is therefore needed.
section-83: Judith Wright's 'Bora Ring': The empty ceremonial ring in the Australian landscape becomes a symbol of the destruction of Aboriginal culture after colonisation. The disappearance of songs, dances and hunters and the reference to Cain's guilt express mourning and the moral responsibility of the settlers.

Margaret Atwood's 'A Sad Child': Speaking frankly to a sad young person, the poet mocks easy explanations and cures for sadness, admits that no one is ever the 'favourite child', and suggests that suffering is part of the human condition shared by all.

Syed Amanuddin's 'Don't Call Me Indo-Anglian': The poet rejects the label imposed by critics on Indian writers in English and asserts his right to his own identity and to English as his creative medium, reflecting postcolonial concerns about language and identity.

Comparison: The three poems come from Australia, Canada and India and deal with cultural loss, emotional pain and identity. They show how poetry gives voice to marginalised peoples and personal experiences across the world.
section-84: Dostoevsky's 'The Christmas Tree and the Wedding': At a children's party, the narrator sees the wealthy Julian Mastakovich calculate the large dowry of a young girl and begin to court her inappropriately, while he mistreats a poor boy. Five years later, he marries the girl, now sixteen and unhappy. The story exposes greed, the exploitation of children and the hypocrisy of respectable society through irony.

Mansfield's 'A Cup of Tea': Rosemary Fell, a rich and fashionable woman, brings home a poor girl to show kindness, imagining herself as a romantic heroine. When her husband praises the girl's beauty, jealousy replaces generosity, and she sends the girl away with money. The story reveals the shallowness of upper-class charity, class barriers and female insecurity.

Techniques: Dostoevsky uses a first-person observer and a time gap to create a shocking ironic ending; Mansfield uses free indirect discourse, symbolic objects (the box, the cup of tea) and an ironic final question.
Common themes: Both stories examine how money and class shape human relationships and how surface respectability hides selfishness.
section-85: Plot: Amir, son of the wealthy Baba, betrays his loyal Hazara friend Hassan by failing to help him when he is assaulted by Assef after the kite tournament and then by framing him for theft. Amir and Baba flee to the USA after the Soviet invasion. Years later, Rahim Khan tells Amir that Hassan was his half-brother and was killed by the Taliban; Amir returns to Afghanistan, confronts Assef and rescues Hassan's son Sohrab.

Characters: Amir (guilt-ridden narrator seeking redemption), Hassan (loyal, honest and forgiving), Baba (strong, generous but hiding a secret), Assef (cruel bully and later Taliban leader), Rahim Khan (wise guide) and Sohrab (traumatised child).

Themes: Guilt, betrayal and redemption; friendship and loyalty; father-son relationships; ethnic discrimination between Pashtuns and Hazaras; the impact of war and exile; and the immigrant experience in America.

Symbols and style: The kite represents both happiness and Amir's betrayal; the pomegranate tree represents friendship; the slingshot links Hassan and Sohrab. Written in first-person narration with flashbacks, the novel brought Afghan history and culture to a global audience.
section-88: The Romantic Age (about 1798-1832) began with the publication of 'Lyrical Ballads' by Wordsworth and Coleridge in 1798. It was influenced by the French Revolution, Rousseau's ideas and the Industrial Revolution.

Features: love of nature, emphasis on imagination and emotion, interest in the supernatural and the medieval, love of liberty, individualism, simple language and subjects from common life. Major poets: Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Shelley and Keats; prose writers include Charles Lamb, Hazlitt and De Quincey; novelists include Jane Austen and Walter Scott.
section-89: The Victorian Age (1837-1901) coincides with the reign of Queen Victoria. It was a period of industrial growth, colonial expansion, scientific progress (Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species', 1859), religious doubt, social reform and the growth of the middle class.

Major writers: poets Tennyson, Robert Browning, Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Matthew Arnold and the Pre-Raphaelites; novelists Charles Dickens, the Brontes, George Eliot, Thackeray and Thomas Hardy; prose writers Carlyle, Ruskin and Newman. Features include moral seriousness, realism, social criticism and the conflict between faith and science.
section-90: The 20th century saw two World Wars, the decline of the British Empire, psychological ideas of Freud, and rapid technological change. Modernism (about 1910-1940) experimented with form and language: stream of consciousness (Virginia Woolf, James Joyce), fragmented poetry (T.S. Eliot's 'The Waste Land') and new techniques.

Other movements include war poetry (Wilfred Owen), the poetry of the 1930s (Auden), the Theatre of the Absurd (Samuel Beckett), the 'Angry Young Men' (John Osborne), postmodernism and postcolonial writing. Themes include alienation, disillusionment, loss of faith, class conflict and identity.
section-91: Written in 1819 near Florence, the poem has five sections, each a sonnet made of four terza rima tercets and a couplet. In parts 1-3 the poet describes the wind's power over leaves on land (driving 'pestilence-stricken multitudes' of leaves and carrying seeds to their 'wintry bed'), clouds in the sky (the approaching storm) and waves in the sea (waking the Mediterranean). The wind is 'Destroyer and Preserver'.

In part 4 the poet wishes to be a leaf, cloud or wave carried by the wind, and cries, 'I fall upon the thorns of life! I bleed!'. In part 5 he asks the wind to make him its lyre and to scatter his words 'like ashes and sparks' among mankind, ending with the hope: 'If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?'. Themes: destruction and regeneration, revolution, the power of poetry, and the poet's despair and hope.
section-92: This is Sonnet 43 from 'Sonnets from the Portuguese' (1850), written for her husband Robert Browning. It is a Petrarchan sonnet (abbaabba cdcdcd) in iambic pentameter. It begins, 'How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.'

She loves him to the depth, breadth and height her soul can reach; as quietly as everyday needs; freely, as men strive for right; purely, as they turn from praise; with the passion of old griefs and childhood faith; with 'the breath, smiles, tears, of all my life'; and if God chooses, she will love him better after death. The repetition of 'I love thee' (anaphora) builds intensity. Themes: spiritual, all-encompassing and eternal love.
section-93: W.H. Auden wrote the poem in 1939 after moving to the USA. It is an epitaph for a citizen identified only by a number ('JS/07 M 378'), erected by the State. Official agencies report that he was a saint in the modern sense: he served the Greater Community, worked in a factory, paid union dues, was popular with friends, bought a newspaper daily, had insurance and a radio, car and refrigerator, held the proper opinions, and had five children.

The poem ends with the ironic questions: 'Was he free? Was he happy? The question is absurd: / Had anything been wrong, we should certainly have heard.' The poem satirises a bureaucratic, conformist society that measures people by statistics and ignores individuality, freedom and happiness.
section-94: Published in 1843, the novella is divided into five 'staves'. Ebenezer Scrooge, a miserly businessman, hates Christmas ('Bah! Humbug!') and treats his clerk Bob Cratchit badly. On Christmas Eve he is visited by the ghost of his former partner Jacob Marley, bound in chains of greed, who warns him that three spirits will visit.

The Ghost of Christmas Past shows him his lonely childhood, his kind employer Fezziwig and his lost love Belle; the Ghost of Christmas Present shows the Cratchit family's joyful Christmas despite poverty, the sick child Tiny Tim, and the children Ignorance and Want; the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come shows his own lonely death and Tiny Tim's death. Scrooge wakes transformed, sends a turkey to the Cratchits, raises Bob's salary and becomes 'a second father' to Tiny Tim. Themes: generosity, redemption, social responsibility and the spirit of Christmas.
section-95: First performed in 1956, the play started the movement of the 'Angry Young Men' and 'kitchen sink drama'. It is set in a one-room flat in the Midlands. Jimmy Porter, a working-class, university-educated young man who runs a sweet stall, is married to Alison, who comes from an upper-middle-class family. His friend Cliff lives with them.

Jimmy constantly attacks Alison, her family and the establishment. Alison's friend Helena arrives, persuades Alison (who is pregnant) to leave, and then becomes Jimmy's mistress. After Alison loses her baby, she returns; Helena leaves, and Jimmy and Alison are reconciled through their 'bear and squirrel' game. Themes: class conflict, post-war disillusionment, anger, frustration, gender relations and the absence of 'good, brave causes'.
section-97: Romantic Age: Beginning with 'Lyrical Ballads' (1798), Romantic writers like Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Shelley and Keats emphasised imagination, emotion, nature, liberty, the supernatural and the individual. Their poetry was a reaction against neoclassical reason and the industrial city.

Victorian Age: During Queen Victoria's reign (1837-1901), Britain experienced industrialisation, empire, scientific discovery and religious doubt. Writers like Tennyson, Browning, Arnold, Dickens, the Brontes, George Eliot and Hardy dealt with morality, social problems, class, faith and doubt, often in a realistic style.

Twentieth century: The World Wars, modern psychology and social change led to modernist experiments by Eliot, Woolf and Joyce, war poetry, the socially conscious poetry of Auden, the Theatre of the Absurd, the Angry Young Men and postmodern and postcolonial writing.
Conclusion: The movement from Romantic idealism to Victorian moral seriousness and then to modern scepticism and experimentation reflects the changing experience of British society.
section-98: Shelley's 'Ode to the West Wind': In five terza rima sonnets, Shelley describes the wind's power over leaves, clouds and waves as 'destroyer and preserver', expresses personal despair ('I fall upon the thorns of life!'), and prays that the wind will spread his revolutionary ideas. The ending, 'If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?', expresses hope for renewal.

Elizabeth Barrett Browning's 'How Do I Love Thee?': This Petrarchan sonnet lists the ways she loves her husband - in depth, breadth, height, freely, purely, passionately and beyond death - using repetition to express spiritual and complete love.

Auden's 'The Unknown Citizen': A satirical epitaph for a model citizen described through statistics and official reports, which ends by questioning his freedom and happiness. It criticises conformity and the loss of individuality in the modern state.
Comparison: The poems show the Romantic belief in nature and the poet's mission, Victorian intensity of personal feeling, and modern irony about bureaucratic society.
section-99: Plot: The miserly Scrooge, visited by Marley's ghost and three spirits on Christmas Eve, sees his past (lonely childhood, Fezziwig's party, lost love Belle), the present (the poor but happy Cratchits and sick Tiny Tim, his nephew Fred's cheerful party, the children Ignorance and Want), and the future (his unmourned death and Tiny Tim's death). He wakes on Christmas morning a changed man.
Character of Scrooge: He changes from a cold, greedy, isolated man to a generous, joyful and caring person, showing that redemption is possible.

Themes and social criticism: Dickens attacks the harsh treatment of the poor in Victorian England, the Poor Law and workhouses, and promotes charity, family, kindness and the Christmas spirit. The Cratchits represent the dignity of poor families.
Style: Supernatural elements, vivid descriptions, humour, sentimentality and a clear moral message make it one of the most popular stories in English literature.
section-100: Plot: In a small Midlands flat, Jimmy Porter rages against his wife Alison, her upper-class family, the church and the establishment, while their friend Cliff tries to keep peace. Alison's friend Helena persuades the pregnant Alison to leave and then becomes Jimmy's mistress. Months later Alison returns after losing her baby; Helena leaves, and Jimmy and Alison reconcile through their private bear-and-squirrel game.

Character of Jimmy: Jimmy is intelligent, educated and passionate but frustrated, bitter and cruel. He represents the post-war generation who felt there were no 'good, brave causes left' and resented the class system.

Themes: Class conflict, anger and frustration of youth, the failure of post-war Britain to provide opportunities, gender relations and emotional suffering, and nostalgia for the Edwardian past (Colonel Redfern).
Significance: The play's realistic setting, raw language and anti-hero introduced 'kitchen sink' realism to the British stage and made Osborne the leading 'Angry Young Man'.
section-103: The word 'essay' comes from the French 'essai', meaning an attempt or trial, first used by Michel de Montaigne (1580). Francis Bacon is called the father of the English essay ('Of Studies', 'Of Truth').

Types of essays: descriptive, narrative, reflective, argumentative, expository, personal (Charles Lamb's 'Essays of Elia') and periodical essays (Addison and Steele). A good essay has unity, coherence, a clear introduction, body and conclusion, and a personal style.
section-104: A biography is based on research using letters, diaries, documents and interviews, and presents the subject's life, achievements, character and times. Boswell's 'Life of Samuel Johnson' (1791) is considered the greatest English biography.

Qualities of a good biography: accuracy, objectivity, vivid portrayal of character, interesting narration and a balance between the person's private and public life. Indian examples include biographies of Gandhi and Nehru.
section-105: An autobiography is written in the first person and presents the writer's memories, experiences, struggles and reflections. Examples include Gandhi's 'The Story of My Experiments with Truth', Nehru's 'An Autobiography', and A.P.J. Abdul Kalam's 'Wings of Fire'.
A memoir is a related form that focuses on specific events or periods rather than the whole life. Autobiography may be subjective, but it gives intimate insight into the writer's mind and times.
section-106: Edgar Allan Poe described the short story as a narrative that can be read at one sitting and produces a 'single effect'. It has a limited number of characters, a single main plot, a concentrated setting and often a twist or surprise ending.
Famous short story writers include Poe, O. Henry, Guy de Maupassant, Anton Chekhov, Katherine Mansfield, R.K. Narayan, Mulk Raj Anand and Ruskin Bond.
section-107: A novella is usually between about 17,500 and 40,000 words. It has more development than a short story but focuses on a single main conflict and a limited number of characters.
Examples include Dickens's 'A Christmas Carol', Joseph Conrad's 'Heart of Darkness', George Orwell's 'Animal Farm', Hemingway's 'The Old Man and the Sea' and Kafka's 'The Metamorphosis'.
section-108: An epistolary novel is told through letters, diary entries, emails or documents. Examples include Samuel Richardson's 'Pamela' (1740) and 'Clarissa', Bram Stoker's 'Dracula' and Alice Walker's 'The Color Purple'.

Letters as literature include Nehru's 'Letters from a Father to His Daughter' and 'Glimpses of World History'. The form creates intimacy, reveals the inner thoughts of characters and allows multiple points of view.
section-109: Nehru wrote this letter on 26 October 1930 from Naini Central Prison to his daughter Indira (later Indira Gandhi) on her 13th birthday. As he could not send a material gift from prison, he sent 'something of the air and mind and spirit', which no prison walls could stop.

He says he does not want to preach or give sermons, because the best way to learn what is right is by talk and discussion. He encourages her to be a brave soldier in India's freedom struggle, to do nothing in secret and to avoid things she would want to hide, to be 'a soldier in India's service', and reminds her of Gandhiji's principles of truth and non-violence. The letter shows Nehru's affection, idealism and patriotism.
section-110: R.K. Narayan (1906-2001) set many stories in the fictional town of Malgudi. In this story, an astrologer sits under a tamarind tree with his props - cowrie shells, a saffron turban, sacred ash and vermilion - and uses shrewd guesswork to tell fortunes. He had left his village years ago after stabbing a man named Guru Nayak in a drunken quarrel, believing he had killed him.

One evening, a stranger challenges him to answer a question. The astrologer recognises him as Guru Nayak, who is searching for the man who tried to kill him. The astrologer, disguised, tells him his attacker died under a lorry four months ago and advises him to return home. At home, he tells his wife that a great load has been lifted from him. Themes: irony, fate, guilt and the deception of astrology; the story ends with a surprise twist.
section-111: Since the prescribed text should be read directly, students should prepare notes under these headings: author background (Sebastian Zumvu as a writer connected with the North-East), plot summary in their own words, list of major and minor characters with key traits, setting (time and place), themes (for example identity, land, community or change, as found in the text), narrative point of view, important quotations, and the significance of the title.

When answering examination questions, refer to specific incidents from the prescribed reading, explain how they develop the themes and characters, and avoid relying on unverified summaries. Discussing the text with teachers and classmates is the best way to confirm details.
section-113: Essay: A short prose composition on a subject expressing the writer's thoughts, from Montaigne and Bacon to Lamb and modern essayists. Types include personal, periodical, reflective, descriptive and argumentative essays.

Biography and autobiography: Biography (e.g. Boswell's 'Life of Johnson') presents another person's life using research; autobiography (e.g. Gandhi's 'My Experiments with Truth', Kalam's 'Wings of Fire') presents the writer's own life in first person, offering intimacy but subjectivity.

Short story and novella: The short story creates a single effect with few characters and one main incident (Poe, O. Henry, Narayan); the novella is longer and more developed but still centred on one conflict ('A Christmas Carol', 'Animal Farm').

Epistolary writing: Letters and diaries used as literary form, as in Richardson's novels and Nehru's letters to Indira, create intimacy and reveal thoughts directly. Knowledge of these forms helps students understand how form shapes content in prose writing.
section-114: A Birthday Letter - content: Written by Nehru from prison on Indira's 13th birthday, the letter offers ideas instead of material gifts. Nehru avoids preaching and prefers discussion, encourages Indira to think about history, freedom and service, to avoid secrecy and to act openly, and to be a brave soldier in India's freedom struggle following Gandhi's ideals.
A Birthday Letter - significance: It shows the epistolary form's ability to combine love, education and moral guidance, and reveals Nehru as a loving father and a committed nationalist.

An Astrologer's Day - content: The astrologer, who has fled his village after a youthful quarrel in which he thought he had killed Guru Nayak, works as a clever fortune-teller in a market. Guru Nayak himself appears as a client seeking revenge. The astrologer tells him that his attacker is dead and sends him home, relieved to know that he is not a murderer.

An Astrologer's Day - themes and technique: Irony, guilt, fate, the human ability to deceive and the surprise ending. Narayan's simple style, vivid description of the market and gentle humour are typical of his Malgudi stories.
section-115: How to prepare: Read the complete prescribed text carefully at least twice. Prepare a chapter-wise or section-wise summary, a character list with qualities and relationships, and notes on setting, conflict, climax and resolution.

Themes and techniques: Identify the major themes that the text itself presents, the narrative point of view, symbols, language and style, and the relevance of the title. Note important quotations with page references.

Writing answers: Answer long questions with an introduction (author and work), body (discussion of themes, characters and incidents with examples from the text) and conclusion (significance). Since this guide does not include a verified synopsis, confirm all details from the prescribed reading and class notes.
